extracted.intended_audience: military commanders, judge advocates, and practitioners responsible for convening or conducting courts-martial
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and interpretive guidance governing who may convene courts-martial, their composition, oath and secrecy requirements, jurisdictional rules, quorum and sentencing limits, and the limited contempt powers of military courts under the Articles of War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corps commander convening authority (separate army requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A corps commander is held to be a commander of an army in the field and may convene a court-martial under the article, but sound policy requires that only the highest military authority in any army have final power to confirm and execute sentences of death and dismissal; the act has not been construed as conferring that power on a corps commander when his command is not a separate and distinct army but only a constituent part of a larger body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the corps is not a separate, distinct army (e.g., part of a larger army such as the Army of the Potomac), the corps commander lacks authority to confirm capital/dismissal sentences; citations include R. 11, 543 (Mar. 1865) and later opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal presence of convening officer not essential
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of legislation or orders forbidding it, personal presence within the territorial limits of his command is not essential to the validity of an order given by a department commander appointing a court-martial within such limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A convening officer may issue valid orders appointing courts-martial even when not physically present in the department, unless prohibited by superior orders or statute. (16 Op. Atty. Gen. (1875) cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff officer authority limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: An assistant adjutant general, or other staff officer of a department commander, is not empowered, of his own authority in the absence of the commander, to relieve an officer duly detailed upon a court-martial by such commander, any more than he is empowered to detail a new officer as a member of such a court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff officers may not unilaterally alter the composition of a court-martial detailed by the commander; see R. 43, 332 (June 1880).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary commander limitation (lieutenant colonel)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lieutenant colonel in temporary command of a territorial division, department, or army, is without authority to appoint a general court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary rank or acting command by certain officers (e.g., lieutenant colonel) does not, by itself, confer authority to convene a general court-martial. (C. 17335, Jan. 7, 1905; others cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Successor lacking convening qualification cannot detail members
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer who is not qualified under the seventy‑second article of war to convene a court-martial cannot issue orders detailing members to a court already appointed, even though he succeed to the command held by the convening officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualification under the relevant article is required to exercise detailing authority; see C. 16710 (Aug. 25, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction follows temporarily operating troops
rubrics_metrics.description: When troops in the prosecution of a practice march or while engaged in a joint encampment or maneuver pass within the territorial limits of a department, they pass, for court-martial purposes, from the jurisdiction of the department in which they are permanently stationed into that of the commander of the department in which they are temporarily operating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary operational control places troops within the temporary department's jurisdiction for purposes of convening and trying courts-martial. (C. 20052, May 9, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Convening officer as accuser/prosecutor determined by animus
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the commander who convened the court is to be regarded as the 'accuser or prosecutor' depends mainly upon his animus in the matter; he may initiate investigation and prefer charges personally and thus be the accuser, or he may properly direct investigation and referral without becoming the accuser in the sense of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors indicating the convening officer is an accuser include personal interest adverse to the accused, adopting another's charges as his own, directing charges despite investigative recommendation against preferring them, and other indicia of personal animus (see C. 2240, May 1896 and multiple R. citations). If claimed, the accused may prove the convening officer's status by affidavit or other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of charges by department commander not automatically making him accuser
rubrics_metrics.description: When superior authority directs the commanding general of a department to bring an officer to trial and leaves details of preparing charges to the department commander, the department commander, by preparing the charges, does not thereby become the accuser within the meaning of the seventy‑second article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish acts taken pursuant to superior direction from personal, adverse initiation; see C. 17212 and C. 17335 (1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Department commander ordering judge advocate to sign charges not accuser
rubrics_metrics.description: When, in the execution of his duties, the department commander orders the department judge advocate to formulate and sign charges made by another, the department commander who is the convening authority does not thereby become the accuser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formal role of preparing or having charges signed by the judge advocate does not equal personal prosecution if done in discharge of official duty. (C. 3913, Mar. 17, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature of charges does not alone make convening officer the accuser
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not essential that the commander who convenes the court-martial for the trial should sign the charges to make him the 'accuser or prosecutor,' nor does the fact that charges were signed by another conclusively determine whether the convening commander is the accuser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legal question concerns the convening officer's personal relation, knowledge, and animus; absence of signature can be overcome by affidavits and proof of circumstances showing personal animus. (Opinion of Atty. Gen. Devens, Aug. 1, 1878, and various R. citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and designation of 'separate brigade'
rubrics_metrics.description: A brigade to be a 'separate brigade' must not exist as a component part of a division; to authorize its commander to convene a general court-martial it must be detached from or disconnected with any division and be operating as a distinct command. Proper designation by higher authority (e.g., an order) is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records lacking evidence that a detachment was designated a 'separate brigade' render proceedings void; an 1864 order directing designation was treated as directory—actual designation suffices even if omitted from convening order, but omission is a serious irregularity. (Multiple R. and C. citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Convening authority discretion on number of officers to detail
rubrics_metrics.description: It is for the convening authority to determine what number of officers can be convened without manifest injury to the service, and his decision in the matter is conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The convening authority's practical judgment on manpower impacts is controlling. (R. 3, 82, June 1863.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum quorum and members for general court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: While a number less than five cannot be organized as a court or proceed with a trial, they may perform preliminary acts; a court may legally proceed so long as five members—the minimum quorum—remain; otherwise where reduced below five it cannot proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less than five may adjourn day-to-day and perform organizational acts; if reduced during trial the court may continue with five. (R. 5, 319; R. 16, 549; C. 22163.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court reduced to four and adjourning does not dissolve the court
rubrics_metrics.description: A court reduced to four members and thereupon adjourning for an indefinite period does not dissolve itself; in adjourning it should report the facts to the convening authority and wait his orders, who may complete it by adding members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The convening authority may complete the court later by adding members and ordering it to reassemble. (R. 5, 319; 39, 328.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferior courts: subject-matter and sentencing limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferior courts have jurisdiction of all military offenses not capital committed by enlisted men, but in view of their limitations to sentence it is generally inexpedient to resort to them for graver offenses (larcencies, aggravated drunkenness, prolonged absences without leave, etc.) where adequate punishment would be beyond their power; inferior courts cannot try capital offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although inferior courts cannot decline to try an offense because of sentencing limits, serious offenses should be referred to general courts; statutory sentence limits apply to single sentences but multiple trials/sentences can exceed those limits in aggregate. (Multiple R. and C. citations; Act of Mar. 2, 1901 noted.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on sentences by inferior courts and permissible alternative punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations imposed by the article refer to single sentences; inferior courts may not for a single sentence exceed statutory caps (e.g., imprisonment/forfeiture limits) but may impose other punishments sanctioned by service usage such as reduction to the ranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: forfeiting pecuniary allowances in addition to pay exceeding one month's pay not authorized; reduction to ranks may be imposed. (R. 29, 401; B. 30, 667; G. 1397.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath of members is essential and must be individual
rubrics_metrics.description: The administering to the court of the prescribed oath is an essential preliminary to its entering upon a trial; the oath shall be taken not by the court as a whole but by each member; until the oath is taken the court is not qualified to try and determine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arraignment and reception of plea before the court is sworn are without legal effect. A member added after the original swearing must be separately sworn in the full form; a member may elect affirmation instead of oath. (R. 38, 196; R. 10, 563; R. 2, 562.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath scope tied to matters before the court at time sworn
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are sworn to try and determine the matter before them at the time of the administering of the oath; if after swearing an additional charge setting forth a new and distinct offense is introduced and tried, the proceedings as to that charge are fatally defective since the court was not sworn to try it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New, distinct charges introduced after the oath require the court to be re-sworn to avoid fatal defects. (R. 24, 513.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy of members' votes and prohibition on recording individual votes
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of secrecy regarding a member's vote is to place him beyond influence when voting; statements of each member's vote in the record are a clear violation of the oath and the oath is violated by disclosure of votes to clerks or statements that all concurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While such violations do not necessarily vitiate the proceedings or sentence, they are grave irregularities and breaches of the oath. (P. 63, 263; R. 2, 59; B. 2, 76.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reopening court after conviction to receive evidence of prior convictions permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: The reopening of the court, after a conviction, to receive evidence of previous convictions is not a violation of the article; the procedure accords with excluding judge advocates from closed sessions to allow accused to be present when evidence of previous convictions is submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is permitted to place prosecution and defense on a more equal footing; cited in P. 63, 49 and C. 3097 (Apr. 1897).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of finding/sentence to clerk is a violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosing the finding and sentence to a clerk by permitting him to remain with the court at final deliberation and enter the judgment in the record is a violation of the oath and a grave irregularity, though not necessarily invalidating the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep final deliberations closed to clerks/staff who are not sworn members; failure to do so is serious. (R. 28, 146.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's contempt power is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of a court-martial to punish for contempt is confined practically to acts done in its immediate presence; a court cannot punish, as for contempt, a civilian witness who appears and declines to testify, nor does it have common-law contempt powers of civil courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If contempt occurs (within the article's description) the proper course is to suspend business, give the party opportunity to be heard, then impose summary punishment if explanation insufficient (confinement in quarters/guardhouse or forfeiture of reasonable pay typical). Judge advocate authority to issue civil process to compel witnesses does not vest contempt power over civilian witnesses in the court. (R. 5, 172; R. 9, 208; R. 30, 361; IL 49, 306.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commanding officer cannot detail himself as a court member
rubrics_metrics.description: A commanding officer is not authorized to detail himself, with two other officers, as a court under this article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-detailing to create a court is impermissible. (R. 24, 263.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-officers and civil employees not eligible as members
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'acting assistant surgeon,' not being an officer of the Army, cannot be detailed on such court; presence of a civil employee does not have the effect of fixing the command as 'different corps' for purposes of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only qualified officers may be detailed as members; civilian employees or non-officer acting appointees are ineligible. (R. 30, 109; R. 81, 483.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of a command with different corps may authorize convening
rubrics_metrics.description: The general term 'other place' includes any locality where a separate command or detachment exists in which different corps of the Army are represented; presence of officers from different arms (e.g., quartermaster, medical, ordnance) might be sufficient to fix the command as one 'where the troops consist of different corps' and empower the commanding officer to order a court-martial under the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a separate command contains enough officers (other than the commander) available for court service; historical practice supports liberal construction in mixed garrison situations. (R. 44, 32; C. 856.)
